title: Can you discover all subclasses of a sealed class at runtime (`getPermittedSubclasses()`)?
shortTitle: Can you discover all subclasses of a sealed class at runtime (`getPermittedSubclasses()`)?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes, for the direct permitted subtypes. The reflection method `Class.getPermittedSubclasses()`, added in Java 17, returns an array of `Class` objects representing the direct permitted subtypes recorded in the sealed class's `PermittedSubclasses` attribute, or `null` if the class is not sealed. You can also check `Class.isSealed()`. This reflects only the directly permitted subtypes — it does not transitively return grandchildren, and for a `non-sealed` branch it cannot enumerate the open, unlisted subclasses beneath it.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps the official closed list of which products may directly be "an Account" filed in head office records. At any time a clerk can pull that exact list and read off the approved direct products — Savings, Current, Loan. The reflection method is that filing-cabinet lookup: it hands you the head-office list of direct variants. But it only lists the direct products; it does not chase down every sub-variant a product might have, and if one product was stamped "open" for partners, the list cannot name the unknown partner products that do not exist on the official sheet.
s1_definition.oneliner: `getPermittedSubclasses()` returns the direct permitted subtypes recorded in the class file at runtime, but only the direct ones — not transitive descendants or open `non-sealed` subclasses.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes, for the direct permitted subtypes. The reflection method `Class.getPermittedSubclasses()`, added in Java 17, returns an array of `Class` objects representing the direct permitted subtypes recorded in the sealed class's `PermittedSubclasses` attribute, or `null` if the class is not sealed. You can also check `Class.isSealed()`. This reflects only the directly permitted subtypes — it does not transitively return grandchildren, and for a `non-sealed` branch it cannot enumerate the open, unlisted subclasses beneath it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps the official closed list of which products may directly be "an Account" filed in head office records. At any time a clerk can pull that exact list and read off the approved direct products — Savings, Current, Loan. The reflection method is that filing-cabinet lookup: it hands you the head-office list of direct variants. But it only lists the direct products; it does not chase down every sub-variant a product might have, and if one product was stamped "open" for partners, the list cannot name the unknown partner products that do not exist on the official sheet.

**One line to remember:** `getPermittedSubclasses()` returns the direct permitted subtypes recorded in the class file at runtime, but only the direct ones — not transitive descendants or open `non-sealed` subclasses.

sections.s2_technical:
When you declare a sealed type, the compiler records its permitted direct subtypes in a class-file attribute called `PermittedSubclasses`. At runtime, reflection exposes this through **`Class.getPermittedSubclasses()`**, which returns a `Class<?>[]` of exactly those direct permitted subtypes. If the class is not sealed, the method returns **`null`**, so you typically guard with `Class.isSealed()` first. For example, `Account.class.isSealed()` returns `true`, and `Account.class.getPermittedSubclasses()` returns the array of its directly permitted subtypes.

The key limitation is that this returns **only the direct** permitted subtypes, matching the `permits` clause (or the same-file inferred set). It does **not** walk the hierarchy transitively. If `Account` permits `LoanAccount`, and `LoanAccount` is itself sealed permitting `HomeLoan` and `CarLoan`, then `Account.class.getPermittedSubclasses()` returns only `LoanAccount` (plus the other direct ones), not `HomeLoan` or `CarLoan`. To get the full leaf set you **recurse**: for each permitted subtype, if it is itself sealed, call `getPermittedSubclasses()` again, descending until you reach `final` leaves or a `non-sealed` branch.

For a **`non-sealed` branch**, the openness means you **cannot enumerate** all actual subclasses at runtime, because new ones can be loaded at any time and are not recorded anywhere. `getPermittedSubclasses()` will list the `non-sealed` type itself (as a direct permitted subtype of its sealed parent), but there is no reflective way to list the unknown classes that extend the `non-sealed` type, since the whole point of `non-sealed` is that the set is open. So complete runtime discovery is only possible for fully closed (`final`/`sealed` all the way down) hierarchies.

This reflective discovery enables several **practical uses**. Frameworks can auto-register serializers for each permitted subtype, validation layers can enumerate the closed set, documentation tools can list variants, and test harnesses can generate a case per subtype. In banking, a serialization layer can derive the Jackson or Gson subtype mappings directly from `getPermittedSubclasses()` so the mapping never drifts out of sync with the sealed `permits` list, which is a real maintenance win.

A senior nuance is that because the permitted set is recorded in the class file and validated by the JVM at load time, `getPermittedSubclasses()` is authoritative and trustworthy — it cannot be fooled by a class that was not actually permitted. Another nuance is that the returned `Class` objects may need the subtypes to be loadable, so reflective discovery triggers or requires their presence; handle `ClassNotFoundException`-style issues in exotic classloading setups. A final nuance is that this reflective closed-set knowledge is what lets you build generic, data-driven handling over a sealed type without hard-coding the variants, so when a new permitted subtype is added, framework code that iterates `getPermittedSubclasses()` picks it up automatically, which pairs beautifully with the compile-time exhaustiveness of switches for application code.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants its serialization layer to register a mapping for every permitted account product automatically, so the mapping never drifts from the sealed `permits` list. We use `getPermittedSubclasses()` to enumerate the direct permitted subtypes at runtime and build the registration.

Problem 2 — The hierarchy is multi-level: `Account` permits `LoanAccount`, which is itself sealed with its own permitted leaves. We need the full leaf set, so we recurse: for each permitted subtype that is itself sealed, we descend until we reach final leaves.

Problem 3 — One branch is `non-sealed` for partner products, and the bank must understand that runtime discovery stops there, because the open branch's subclasses cannot be enumerated. We show the recursion stopping at the `non-sealed` type and explain why.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `Account` permitting a final `SavingsAccount`, a sealed `LoanAccount` (permitting final `HomeLoan` and `CarLoan`), and a `non-sealed PartnerProduct`. We write a `SealedScanner` that uses `isSealed` and `getPermittedSubclasses` recursively to print the full discoverable set, and log the results.

The code contains: the multi-level sealed hierarchy and a recursive `SealedScanner` with a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sealed `Account` type whose permitted set we discover reflectively at runtime.

Step 1 — The code checks `Account.class.isSealed()`, which returns true because the class file carries the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute. This guards the discovery, since a non-sealed class would return null from `getPermittedSubclasses()`.

Step 2 — The code calls `Account.class.getPermittedSubclasses()` and prints the direct permitted subtypes: savings account, loan account, and partner product. This is one level only — it does not include the loan leaves yet.

Step 3 — The recursive scanner then descends. For `Account` (sealed) it visits each permitted subtype. Savings account is final, so it is logged as a final leaf. Loan account is itself sealed, so the scanner recurses into it and discovers its permitted leaves, home loan and car loan, both final.

Step 4 — When the scanner reaches the partner product, it finds the type is not sealed and not final, so it is a `non-sealed` open branch. Discovery stops there with a note that its subclasses cannot be enumerated, because new partner subclasses can be loaded at any time and are not recorded anywhere.

Step 5 — Finally the code confirms `PartnerProduct.class.isSealed()` is false, reinforcing that the open branch has no reflectively-discoverable closed set. The output shows the full closed portion plus the stopping point at the open branch.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, I can discover the permitted subtypes of a sealed class at runtime using the reflection method getPermittedSubclasses, added in Java 17. It returns an array of Class objects for the direct permitted subtypes that the compiler recorded in the sealed class's PermittedSubclasses attribute, and it returns null if the class is not sealed, so I usually guard it with isSealed first. Because the permitted set is written into the class file and validated by the JVM at load time, this reflective view is authoritative and cannot be fooled by a class that was not actually permitted.

The key limitation is that it returns only the direct permitted subtypes, matching the permits clause. It does not walk the hierarchy transitively. In my banking project Account permits a loan account that is itself sealed with its own leaves, home loan and car loan, so calling getPermittedSubclasses on Account returns only the loan account, not its leaves. To get the full leaf set I recurse: for each permitted subtype, if it is itself sealed I call getPermittedSubclasses again, descending until I hit final leaves.

The recursion has to stop at a non-sealed branch, and this is an important point. Because a non-sealed type reopens its branch, its subclasses are open and can be loaded at any time, and they are not recorded anywhere, so there is no reflective way to enumerate them. In my model the partner product is non-sealed, so my scanner lists it but reports that its subclasses cannot be discovered. That means complete runtime discovery is only possible for hierarchies that are closed all the way down with final and sealed types.

Where this really pays off is building data-driven framework code. In my serialization layer I derive the Jackson subtype mappings directly from getPermittedSubclasses, so the mapping can never drift out of sync with the sealed permits list, and when a new permitted product is added the registration picks it up automatically. Validation layers, documentation generators, and test harnesses can all enumerate the closed set the same way. So reflective discovery gives me the runtime closed-set knowledge, and it pairs beautifully with the compile-time exhaustiveness of switches, giving me both automatic framework wiring and compiler-checked application code over the same sealed hierarchy.
